summary: Reports on two workshops, held under IAB auspices, about the technical support of policy issues that arise when interconnecting networks. The work supported the Federal Research Internet Coordinating Committee in building an interconnected set of networks for the research community.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1124 reports on two workshops about connecting federal research networks with different policies. The report organizes technical and policy issues into areas including access control, resource sharing, and security services.

questions: what policy issues arise when interconnecting networks
what were the rfc 1124 workshop topics
subtitle: Workshop findings on policies and technology for interconnecting research networks.

tldr.problem: Federal research networks had different use policies, but their agencies wanted to interconnect them and share network resources.
tldr.mechanism: Two workshops examined policy statements, network access control, fair resource sharing, and end-to-end services, organizing possible capabilities into phases.
tldr.outcome: The report provides a roadmap of issues, experiments, and research areas for interconnecting the networks while considering agency policies.

today: RFC 1124 reports the results of workshops held in 1988 on technical support for interconnecting research networks. It records issues and proposed phased activities rather than defining a network protocol.

sections.title: The Interconnection Goal and Workshops
sections.content:
The workshops supported the Federal Research Internet Coordinating Committee's work on an interconnected set of networks for research. Agencies wanted to share connectivity and resources while retaining their own missions and rules for network use.

The report groups capability into four phases: currently available techniques, capabilities deployed at limited sites, understood capabilities needing development, and capabilities requiring research. Four working groups examined policies, network access control, resource sharing, and end-to-end services.
sections.plainLanguage: The agencies wanted a connected research network, but each had its own policies. The workshops described a phased path from available tools to capabilities needing more development or research.

sections.title: Agency Policies
sections.content:
The policy working group documented the different purposes and restrictions of participating agencies. Examples included research and education use, rules about commercial use, accounting for shared facilities, and restrictions on connections to other networks.

The report says making all agency rules identical was not the goal. Instead, those policies were the basis for the technical groups' work on interconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: The agencies had different rules for acceptable network use. The workshops documented those differences rather than trying to make every policy the same.

sections.title: Access Control Across Networks
sections.content:
The access-control group considered how to apply administrative policies to network paths and resources. The report discusses policy gateways, route information, authentication, labels, and trust between domains that would enforce the policies.

It notes that connection-oriented exchanges offer a natural point for authorization checks, while brief transaction traffic and multicast create different challenges. The report discusses auditing as an additional measure and says perfect access mediation may be infeasible.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks need ways to check whether traffic may use shared paths. The workshops considered gateways, credentials, packet information, and the trust needed between administrative domains.

sections.title: Resource Sharing and End-to-End Services
sections.content:
The resource-sharing group considered service classes, user categories, accounting, and fair bandwidth use. The report identifies a difficulty: a local gateway decision can affect routes across the network, so some policies may require global routing support.

The end-to-end security group discusses authentication, access control, integrity, confidentiality, and service assurance across administrative domains. Its phased activities range from existing tools such as passwords and mail relays to longer-term work on certificates, key management, distributed services, and policy routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Agencies wanted to share bandwidth fairly and provide compatible security across network boundaries. The report lists immediate steps and longer-term work, including global routing support.
